Adding methods and tools

Source: vignettes/extending_giotto.Rmd
extending_giotto.Rmd

This guide describes how to add an external spatial method to the Giotto Suite, either by reimplementing it natively or by connecting the original tool. It reuses what the Suite already has: the five analysis verbs and their Param classes, the setters for every slot, the analysis history, and package_check() for tools that are installed only when used. No method needs its own package, and nothing is installed for users who never run it.

1 Three kinds of integration

  • A native reimplementation recomputes a published method inside Giotto, built from Suite building blocks. The BANKSY embedding (runNeighborhoodPCA()) is the example: a stored spatial network, the Suite’s PCA, and only BANKSY’s neighbour weights and gradient as new code. It lives in Giotto.
  • An engine package holds a method’s computation in its own small R package with no Giotto dependency, and Giotto adds the Param, the verb method and the wrapper. HMRF (spatialHMRF, used by runHMRF()) and spatialDWLS work this way. Use it when the engine is substantial, useful on its own, or credited to other authors; the package is in Giotto’s Suggests and checked when the method runs.
  • A connection runs the original tool and moves data in and out, for example ONTraC (Python) or CellChat (R). It lives in GiottoConnect, one file per tool: R/tool-<name>.R.

2 Reuse before writing

Build on what the Suite already has and write only what is specific to the method. Spatial neighbours come from a stored spatial network (createSpatialNetwork()), PCA from reduceData(x, pcaParam()), clustering from the existing clustering functions. BANKSY’s native embedding adds only its neighbour weights and gradient (neighborhood_operators()) on top of a stored kNN network. If an existing building block is too slow for the new method, improve it there rather than working around it.

3 Verbs return, wrappers write

Each method is a Param class plus a method on one of the five verbs, chosen by what it returns:

Verb Returns
processData() values of the same shape (normalized, smoothed)
filterData() the IDs to keep
reduceData() an embedding or decomposition
clusterData() one label per cell
analyzeData() statistics and other outputs

The method on a data class (a matrix, a table) returns what its verb promises and never touches a giotto object. A thin run<Name>() wrapper reads the inputs from the giotto object, calls the verb, and writes the result with the existing setters.

4 Where results go

Results go into the slots that already exist:

Output Slot Written with
a label or value per cell cell metadata addCellMetadata()
a value per feature feature metadata addFeatMetadata()
cells x dimensions dimension reduction createDimObj() + setDimReduction()
cells x categories (proportions, probabilities) spatial enrichment createSpatEnrObj() + setSpatialEnrichment()
features x cells values expression setExpression()
a graph on expression or an embedding nearest-neighbour network setNearestNetwork()
a spatial graph spatial network setSpatialNetwork()
anything else (interaction tables, fitted models, tool objects) none returned to the caller

5 Plots

Results in existing slots can be drawn with existing plots, so most integrations need none of their own. ONTraC is the example: niche clusters with spatPlot2D(cell_color = ), their probabilities with spatCellPlot2D(spat_enr_names = ), NT scores per cell type with ridgePlot(group_by = ), and cell type composition with plotLabelComposition(). List these in the wrapper’s help page.

When a tool has a view no Giotto plot covers, and that view only makes sense for this tool, add one plot function to the tool’s file:

  • name it plot<Tool><What>(), as plotONTraCConnectivity() (the graph of ONTraC’s niche clusters);
  • read what it draws from the slots the wrapper wrote (for ONTraC, the spatial enrichment’s misc), never from the tool’s output files;
  • put ggplot2 (and any other plotting package) in Suggests, check it with package_check(), and return through GiottoVisuals::plot_output_handler() so show_plot, return_plot and save_plot work as in the other Giotto plots.

A view that several tools would use belongs in GiottoVisuals instead.

6 Recording what was run

The wrapper ends with

update_giotto_params(gobject, description = "_<name>",
    attachments = list(param = param))

so the analysis history keeps the Param with its settings. A Param holds settings only, never data.

7 Dependencies

  • The tool is never in Imports. A CRAN or Bioconductor tool goes in Suggests. A tool only on GitHub gets an install hint from package_check(repository = "github:owner/repo") and is called with getExportedValue(), so R CMD check stays clean; the Suite’s own engine packages (spatialHMRF, spatialDWLS) go in Suggests and Remotes. Every tool is checked with package_check() when the function runs.
  • Python tools run in a separate R session through GiottoUtils::py_run() (or py_run_cli() for a command line program), in an environment built on first use, so tools with conflicting requirements can be used side by side. Pin the tool’s version, and record the returned py_versions with the Param.
  • Tests use skip_if_not_installed(), so a broken tool release breaks only its own function.
  • A function shared with another package is exported as a documented snake_case utility, not reached with :::.

8 Names and credit

  • The Param class is named after the method: ontracParam, cellchatParam, hmrfParam. A connection’s or engine package’s wrapper is run<Method>().
  • A native reimplementation gets a descriptive name, not the tool’s, so a wrapper of the original can sit beside it: runNeighborhoodPCA() next to GiottoConnect::runBanksy().
  • Its help page names the original method and paper under @references, asks users to cite it, and says how it differs from the original and how closely it matches.

9 Checking an integration

  • Compare against the original tool on the same input, with a seed, keep the comparison script outside the package (for example in examples/<tool>_comparison/), and report the difference in the pull request.
  • A pull request adds one method. Changes to other methods or shared helpers, even improvements, go in a pull request of their own, so each can be reviewed and reverted alone.
  • GiottoConnect::checkGiottoMethod() (and expect_giotto_method() in tests) checks a wrapper against these rules: which slots it wrote, that the history holds its Param, and that its help page has references.
